## 1. Topic Introduction — What Are Biomolecules and Why Do They Matter?

**Biomolecules** are the carbon-based chemical compounds that make up every living cell and carry out every process we call "life". A cell is not a bag of random chemicals — it is a highly organised factory built from a small, special set of molecules: **carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, minerals, enzymes and water**.

Why this topic is the foundation of all of Biology:

- **Structure:** every cell wall, membrane, cytoskeleton and chromosome is built from biomolecules.
- **Energy:** every beat of your heart, every nerve impulse and every cell division is powered by the chemical energy stored in carbohydrates and lipids.
- **Information:** nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) store and translate the hereditary instructions that make a mango tree a mango tree and you, you.
- **Regulation:** enzymes (proteins) control the speed of every chemical reaction; minerals and water create the environment in which those reactions can happen.
- **Connection to the syllabus:** this topic directly feeds into *cell structure* (membranes are phospholipids + proteins), *cell division* (chromosomes are DNA + proteins), *enzymes* (all of metabolism), and later units like *ecology* (energy flow is chemical energy flowing through biomolecules).

**Where biomolecules come from:** almost all biomolecules are ultimately built by **photosynthesis**, which converts CO₂ and H₂O into glucose. Animals cannot make all of their own biomolecules from scratch — they must eat plants or other animals. This is why biomolecules are also the chemical basis of **food chains**.

## 2. Fundamental Conceptual Understanding — The Chemical Basis of Life

### 2.1 The elements of life

Over 99% of living matter is made of just six elements: **C, H, O, N, P, S** (remember: **CHNOPS**), plus minerals in smaller amounts.

| Element | Role in biomolecules |
|---|---|
| Carbon (C) | Backbone of all organic molecules — forms 4 stable covalent bonds |
| Hydrogen (H) | Part of every organic molecule; electron carrier in respiration |
| Oxygen (O) | Oxidation, water, carbohydrates, energy release |
| Nitrogen (N) | Amino acids, proteins, nucleic acid bases |
| Phosphorus (P) | Nucleic acids, ATP, phospholipids, bone |
| Sulphur (S) | Some amino acids (cysteine, methionine), protein shape |

**Why carbon?** Carbon has exactly 4 valence electrons, so it can form four strong covalent bonds, bond to itself in chains and rings, and build enormous, stable yet versatile molecules. Silicon, the closest alternative, forms weaker bonds and cannot build the diversity of molecules life needs. This is the deepest reason life is carbon-based.

### 2.2 The monomer → polymer principle

Almost every large biomolecule (macromolecule) is a **polymer** — a chain of repeated small units called **monomers**, joined by a specific covalent bond.

| Biomolecule class | Monomer (building block) | Polymer / large form | Bond joining monomers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrates | Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose) | Disaccharides, polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) | Glycosidic bond |
| Proteins | Amino acids (20 standard types) | Polypeptides → proteins | Peptide bond (−CO−NH−) |
| Lipids | Glycerol + fatty acids | Triglycerides, phospholipids | Ester bond (−COO−) |
| Nucleic acids | Nucleotides | DNA, RNA | Phosphodiester bond |

**Key conceptual point:** lipids (triglycerides) are *often listed* with the macromolecules but are **not true polymers** — fatty acids are not repeated identical monomers joined head-to-tail the way glucose or amino acids are. This is a favourite NEB trick question.

### 2.3 How polymers are built and broken: condensation and hydrolysis

- **Condensation (dehydration synthesis):** two monomers are joined and one molecule of **water is removed**. Building reactions — e.g. glucose + glucose → maltose + H₂O.
- **Hydrolysis:** water is added to split the polymer back into monomers. Breaking reactions — digestion is entirely hydrolysis.

$$\text{monomer}_1\text{–OH} + \text{HO–monomer}_2 \;\xrightarrow{\text{condensation}}\; \text{monomer}_1\text{–monomer}_2 + H_2O$$

**Cause and effect:** condensation requires energy (anabolic, enzyme-driven), hydrolysis releases it (catabolic). A polypeptide of *n* amino acids contains **(n − 1)** peptide bonds and loses **(n − 1)** water molecules during synthesis — a standard numerical asked in NEB exams.

### 2.4 Organic vs inorganic compounds in the cell

| Basis | Organic compounds | Inorganic compounds |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Carbon-based compounds (except simple ones like CO₂, carbonates) associated with living systems | Compounds without carbon skeletons (water, minerals, salts, gases) |
| Examples | Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, enzymes, vitamins | Water, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Fe²⁺, PO₄³⁻, O₂, CO₂ |
| Size | Usually large, complex macromolecules | Usually small, simple molecules or ions |
| Burning / combustion | Burn to give CO₂ + H₂O + energy | Generally do not burn |
| Function in cell | Build structures, store information, catalyse reactions, store energy | Provide medium, pH balance, osmotic balance, cofactors |
| Percentage of cell | ~20–30% (dry weight mostly organic) | Water alone is 70–90% of a cell |

## 3. Carbohydrates — The Primary Energy and Structural Molecules

### 3.1 Definition and general formula

**Carbohydrates** are organic compounds of **C, H and O** in which hydrogen and oxygen occur in the same 2:1 ratio as in water. General formula: **Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ** — e.g. glucose C₆H₁₂O₆, sucrose C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. They are also called **saccharides** (Greek *sakcharon* = sugar). They are the **first products of photosynthesis** and the main immediate fuel of respiration.

### 3.2 Classification of carbohydrates

| Class | Number of sugar units | Solubility / taste | Examples | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monosaccharides | 1 (cannot be hydrolysed) | Soluble, sweet, crystalline | Glucose, fructose, galactose, ribose | Immediate energy currency; monomers of all carbohydrates |
| Disaccharides | 2 (one glycosidic bond) | Soluble, sweet, crystalline | Maltose (glc+glc), sucrose (glc+fru), lactose (glc+gal) | Transport sugars (sucrose in plants), milk sugar (lactose) |
| Oligosaccharides | 3–10 | Partially soluble | Raffinose, stachyose | Cell-recognition markers on membrane surfaces |
| Polysaccharides | >10 (hundreds–thousands) | Insoluble or colloidal, tasteless | Starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin, inulin | Energy storage and structural materials |

**Monosaccharides are further classified by carbon number:**

| Carbon number | Name | Example | Importance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | Triose | Glyceraldehyde | Intermediate of respiration (glycolysis) |
| 5 | Pentose | Ribose, deoxyribose | Sugars of RNA and DNA |
| 6 | Hexose | Glucose, fructose, galactose | Main metabolic fuel |
| 7 | Heptose | Sedoheptulose | Photosynthesis (Calvin cycle) intermediate |

### 3.3 The glycosidic bond and how disaccharides form

A **glycosidic bond** is the C–O–C covalent link formed between two monosaccharides by **condensation**, catalysed by enzymes. Glucose + glucose → maltose + H₂O; glucose + fructose → sucrose; glucose + galactose → lactose.

### 3.4 Reducing vs non-reducing sugars — a guaranteed exam comparison

| Basis | Reducing sugars | Non-reducing sugars |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Have a free (or potentially free) aldehyde or ketone group that can reduce Cu²⁺ | No free aldehyde/ketone group; the anomeric carbons are locked in the glycosidic bond |
| Examples | All monosaccharides (glucose, fructose), maltose, lactose | Sucrose, all polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) |
| Benedict's / Fehling's test | Positive — brick-red Cu₂O precipitate | Negative (sucrose must first be hydrolysed, then it turns positive) |
| Biological role | Readily oxidised in respiration | Storage or transport forms (sucrose is non-reducing so it does not react while being transported in phloem) |

### 3.5 Storage vs structural polysaccharides

| Basis | Storage polysaccharides | Structural polysaccharides |
|---|---|---|
| Function | Energy reserve, broken down when glucose is needed | Mechanical support and protection |
| Examples | Starch (plants), glycogen (animals, liver + muscle), inulin (dahlia tubers) | Cellulose (plant cell wall), chitin (fungal wall, arthropod exoskeleton), peptidoglycan (bacterial wall) |
| Glucose linkage | α-1,4 and α-1,6 glycosidic bonds (α configuration) | β-1,4 glycosidic bonds (β configuration) |
| Digestibility | Human-digestible (we have α-amylase) | Not digestible by humans (we lack cellulase) — cellulose is "roughage/fibre" |
| Iodine test | Starch: blue-black; glycogen: reddish-brown | No colour with iodine |

**Conceptual insight:** the *only* chemical difference between digestible starch and indigestible cellulose is the **α vs β configuration** of the glycosidic bond — a beautiful example of how molecular geometry controls biology.

### 3.6 Functions of carbohydrates

1. **Energy source:** 4 kcal/g; glucose is the universal fuel of respiration.
2. **Energy storage:** starch (plants), glycogen (animals).
3. **Structural material:** cellulose in cell walls, chitin in fungi and arthropods.
4. **Precursors:** carbon skeletons for amino acids, fatty acids, nucleotides.
5. **Transport:** sucrose moves food through phloem.
6. **Cell recognition:** oligosaccharides on cell surfaces (blood groups, immunity).
7. **Component of nucleic acids:** ribose and deoxyribose.

## 4. Proteins — The Working Molecules of the Cell

### 4.1 Definition and building blocks

**Proteins** are large polymers of **amino acids** joined by **peptide bonds**. The word comes from Greek *proteios* = "of first importance" (coined by Berzelius). Proteins make up ~50% of a cell's dry weight and perform more different jobs than any other biomolecule class.

**Amino acid structure:** every standard amino acid has a central (α-) carbon bonded to four groups:

1. An **amino group** (−NH₂) — basic
2. A **carboxyl group** (−COOH) — acidic
3. A **hydrogen atom**
4. A variable **R-group (side chain)** — this alone defines which amino acid it is

Because of the amino and carboxyl groups, amino acids are **amphoteric** — they act as both acid and base, existing as **zwitterions** in solution. There are **20 standard amino acids**; humans cannot synthesise about 9–10 of them (**essential amino acids** — must come from diet, e.g. lysine, tryptophan, methionine).

### 4.2 The peptide bond — how proteins form

The −COOH of one amino acid condenses with the −NH₂ of the next, releasing water and forming the **peptide bond (−CO−NH−)**:

$$H_2N\text{–}CH(R)\text{–}COOH + H_2N\text{–}CH(R')\text{–}COOH \rightarrow H_2N\text{–}CH(R)\text{–}CO\text{–}NH\text{–}CH(R')\text{–}COOH + H_2O$$

Two amino acids → **dipeptide**; many → **polypeptide**; one or more folded polypeptides → **protein**. A chain of *n* amino acids has **(n − 1)** peptide bonds.

### 4.3 The four levels of protein structure

| Level | What it is | Bonds involved | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | The linear sequence of amino acids (covalent chain) | Peptide bonds | Insulin's 51-amino-acid sequence |
| Secondary | Local coiling/folding of the chain | Hydrogen bonds | α-helix (keratin), β-pleated sheet (silk fibroin) |
| Tertiary | Overall 3-D shape of one whole polypeptide | H-bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide (S–S) bridges, hydrophobic interactions | Myoglobin, enzymes |
| Quaternary | Assembly of 2 or more polypeptide subunits | Same non-covalent forces between subunits | Haemoglobin (4 subunits), insulin (2 chains) |

**Key concept:** **structure determines function.** Change the sequence (primary structure) — as in sickle-cell anaemia, where one wrong amino acid in haemoglobin's β-chain changes the whole shape — and the protein's function collapses.

### 4.4 Classification of proteins

| Main category | Subcategory | Characteristics | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simple proteins | Albumins, globulins, histones, glutelins | Only amino acids on hydrolysis | Egg albumin, serum globulin, histones of chromosomes |
| Conjugated proteins | Glycoproteins, lipoproteins, phosphoproteins, chromoproteins, metalloproteins, nucleoproteins | Protein + a non-protein **prosthetic group** | Mucin (glyco-), lipoproteins of membranes, casein (phospho-), haemoglobin (chromo-: haem + globin), nucleoproteins of chromosomes |
| Derived proteins | Proteoses, peptones, peptides | Partial breakdown products of proteins | Peptones formed during digestion |

### 4.5 Functions of proteins (with examples — learn the pairing)

| Function | Explanation | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Enzymatic (catalytic) | Speed up every metabolic reaction | Amylase, pepsin, DNA polymerase |
| Transport | Carry molecules in blood/membranes | Haemoglobin (O₂), membrane carriers |
| Structural | Build body and cell frameworks | Collagen, keratin, elastin |
| Contractile | Movement, muscle contraction | Actin, myosin |
| Hormonal | Chemical messengers | Insulin, growth hormone |
| Defensive | Immunity | Antibodies (immunoglobulins) |
| Storage | Nutrient reservoirs | Ovalbumin (egg), zein (maize) |
| Toxic / protective | Defence molecules | Snake venom, ricin |
| Buffering | Resist pH change in blood | Plasma proteins, haemoglobin |

### 4.6 Denaturation

**Denaturation** is the loss of a protein's natural 3-D structure (secondary → quaternary) by heat, pH extremes, or chemicals — **peptide bonds are NOT broken**, so the primary sequence survives, but the protein loses its biological activity (boiled egg; curdled milk). Renaturation is possible in some proteins if the denaturing agent is removed.

**Tests:** Biuret test (violet colour — peptide bonds), Xanthoproteic test (yellow with HNO₃ — aromatic amino acids), Million's test (for tyrosine).

## 5. Lipids — Concentrated Energy and Membrane Bricks

### 5.1 Definition

**Lipids** are a heterogeneous group of organic compounds that are **insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents** (ether, chloroform, benzene). They contain C, H, O — but with far less oxygen than carbohydrates, which is why they yield **more than twice the energy (9 kcal/g vs 4 kcal/g)** on oxidation.

### 5.2 Classification of lipids

| Main category | What it is | Examples | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simple lipids | Esters of fatty acids with alcohols | Fats (glycerol + fatty acids = triglycerides), waxes (fatty acid + long-chain alcohol, e.g. beeswax, cuticle wax) | Energy storage; waterproofing |
| Compound (conjugated) lipids | Lipid + non-lipid group | Phospholipids (phosphate + nitrogen base), glycolipids (carbohydrate), lipoproteins (protein) | Membrane structure; blood lipid transport |
| Derived lipids | Products of hydrolysis of simple/compound lipids | Fatty acids, glycerol, steroids (cholesterol, oestrogen, testosterone), terpenes (vitamin A, K, carotenoids) | Hormones, vitamins, membranes |

### 5.3 Fatty acids — saturated vs unsaturated (guaranteed exam table)

| Basis | Saturated fatty acids | Unsaturated fatty acids |
|---|---|---|
| Carbon–carbon bonds | Only single bonds (C–C) | One or more double bonds (C=C) |
| Hydrogen atoms | Maximum possible ("saturated" with H) | Fewer H atoms |
| Physical state at room temp | Solid fats (straight chains pack tightly) | Liquid oils (kinks prevent tight packing) |
| Source | Animal fats — ghee, butter, lard | Plant oils — mustard, sunflower, fish oil |
| Health effect | Raise blood cholesterol, linked to heart disease | Considered healthier; essential fatty acids (linoleic, linolenic) cannot be synthesised by humans |
| Example | Palmitic acid (C₁₆), stearic acid (C₁₈) | Oleic acid (C₁₈, one double bond), linoleic acid (two double bonds) |

### 5.4 Triglycerides — the storage fat

One **glycerol** (a 3-carbon alcohol with 3 −OH groups) + **3 fatty acids** → **triglyceride** + 3 H₂O, via three **ester bonds (−COO−)**. Stored in adipose tissue; the body's most concentrated energy reserve.

### 5.5 Phospholipids — why membranes form (conceptual core)

A phospholipid = glycerol + 2 fatty acids + **phosphate group + nitrogen base**. It is **amphipathic**: a **hydrophilic (water-loving) phosphate head** and **two hydrophobic (water-fearing) fatty-acid tails**. In water, heads face the water and tails hide from it — so phospholipids spontaneously form a **bilayer**, the universal framework of every biological membrane. This directly explains why the fluid-mosaic membrane exists (connect to Topic 3).

### 5.6 Functions of lipids

1. **Concentrated energy storage** — 9 kcal/g; 1 g fat ≈ energy of ~2.25 g carbohydrate.
2. **Membrane structure** — phospholipid bilayer.
3. **Insulation and padding** — subcutaneous fat conserves heat and cushions organs.
4. **Hormones and vitamins** — steroid hormones (oestrogen, testosterone, cortisol); fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K.
5. **Waterproofing** — waxes on leaf cuticles, skin oils.
6. **Electrical insulation** — myelin sheath (lipid) around neurons.
7. **Metabolic water** — oxidised fat yields metabolic water (desert animals, camel hump — the hump stores fat, not water).

**Tests:** Sudan III / IV stain (red), translucent-spot test on paper, saponification (soap formation with NaOH).

## 6. Nucleic Acids — The Information Molecules

### 6.1 Definition and the nucleotide

**Nucleic acids** (DNA and RNA) are polymers of **nucleotides** — the molecules that store, transmit and express hereditary information. First isolated by **Friedrich Miescher (1868–69)** from pus cells as "nuclein".

Every nucleotide has **three parts**:

1. A **pentose sugar** — ribose (RNA) or deoxyribose (DNA, missing one O on C-2′)
2. A **nitrogenous base** — purines (**Adenine, Guanine** — double ring) or pyrimidines (**Cytosine, Thymine, Uracil** — single ring)
3. A **phosphate group** — gives the molecule its acidic character

**Nucleoside = sugar + base. Nucleotide = sugar + base + phosphate.** Nucleotides join by **phosphodiester bonds** between the sugar of one and the phosphate of the next, forming a sugar–phosphate backbone with bases sticking inward.

**ATP (adenosine triphosphate)** is itself a nucleotide — proof that nucleotides are also the energy currency of the cell, not just genetic material.

### 6.2 DNA vs RNA — the master comparison (asked almost every year)

| Basis | DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) | RNA (ribonucleic acid) |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | Deoxyribose | Ribose |
| Strands | Double-stranded (double helix) | Usually single-stranded |
| Bases | A, G, C, **T** (thymine) | A, G, C, **U** (uracil replaces thymine) |
| Location | Mainly nucleus (also mitochondria, chloroplasts) | Nucleus and cytoplasm (ribosomes) |
| Function | Stores hereditary information; self-replicating | Transfers information from DNA to ribosomes; helps protein synthesis |
| Stability | Very stable (deoxyribose + thymine resist damage) | Less stable, short-lived |
| Types | One basic type (but different helix forms) | mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snRNA |
| Length | Very long (millions of nucleotides) | Much shorter |
| Base pairing | A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds) | A=U, G≡C |

### 6.3 Watson–Crick double-helix model (1953) — salient features

1. DNA is a **double helix** of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands (one 5′→3′, the other 3′→5′).
2. The **sugar–phosphate backbones face outside**; the bases pair **inside** the helix.
3. **Complementary base pairing:** A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds), G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds) — a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, keeping the helix a uniform 2 nm wide.
4. The two strands are **complementary** — knowing one sequence fixes the other; this is the physical basis of accurate replication.
5. One complete turn occurs every **3.4 nm** with **10 base pairs per turn**.
6. **Chargaff's rule:** in any DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C (follows directly from pairing).

### 6.4 Types and roles of RNA

| RNA type | Full form | Role |
|---|---|---|
| mRNA | Messenger RNA | Carries the genetic code from DNA to the ribosome |
| tRNA | Transfer RNA | Brings specific amino acids to the ribosome; reads the code |
| rRNA | Ribosomal RNA | Structural + catalytic core of ribosomes |
| snRNA | Small nuclear RNA | RNA splicing in eukaryotes |

### 6.5 Functions of nucleic acids

1. **Storage of genetic information** (DNA).
2. **Transmission of heredity** from parents to offspring and cell to daughter cell.
3. **Expression of information** — DNA → RNA → protein (the central dogma).
4. **Mutation and evolution** — changes in DNA sequence create variation.
5. **Energy transfer** — ATP, NAD, FAD are nucleotide derivatives.

**Test:** diphenylamine reagent turns blue with DNA (Dische test).

## 7. Minerals — The Inorganic Regulators

Minerals are inorganic elements needed in small amounts. They come from food and soil (plants absorb them as ions) and act as **structural materials, cofactors, and osmotic/electrolyte regulators**.

| Mineral (ion) | Category | Key functions | Deficiency effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calcium (Ca²⁺) | Macro | Bones, teeth, muscle contraction, blood clotting, cell-wall middle lamellum | Rickets, poor bones, poor clotting |
| Phosphorus (P) | Macro | ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids, bones | Weak bones, low energy metabolism |
| Iron (Fe²⁺) | Micro | Haemoglobin, cytochromes, chlorophyll synthesis (activator) | Anaemia |
| Iodine (I) | Micro | Thyroxine synthesis | Goitre |
| Sodium (Na⁺) / Potassium (K⁺) | Macro | Nerve impulse, osmotic balance, stomatal movement (K⁺) | Muscle cramps, poor nerve conduction |
| Magnesium (Mg²⁺) | Macro | Central atom of chlorophyll; enzyme activator | Chlorosis |
| Chlorine (Cl⁻) | Micro | Osmotic balance, HCl in gastric juice | Electrolyte imbalance |
| Zinc (Zn²⁺), Copper (Cu²⁺), Manganese (Mn) | Micro | Enzyme cofactors (e.g. Zn for carbonic anhydrase) | Poor growth, enzyme failure |

**Macro vs micro minerals:** macro minerals are needed in larger amounts (>100 mg/day, e.g. Ca, P, Na, K, Mg, Cl); micro (trace) elements are needed in traces but are still essential (Fe, I, Zn, Cu, Mn, Co, Se).

## 8. Enzymes — Biological Catalysts

### 8.1 Definition and nature

**Enzymes** are biological catalysts — almost always **globular proteins** (a few RNAs, "ribozymes", also catalyse) — that **accelerate biochemical reactions thousands to millions of times** without being consumed themselves. The term was coined by **Kühne (1878)**; **Sumner (1926)** crystallised the first enzyme, urease, and proved enzymes are protein.

**Terminology chain:** some enzymes need a non-protein helper to work:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Apoenzyme | The inactive protein part alone |
| Cofactor | Non-protein helper: metal ion (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺) |
| Coenzyme | Organic cofactor, often a vitamin derivative (NAD, FAD, coenzyme A) |
| Prosthetic group | Cofactor tightly/covalently bound to the apoenzyme |
| Holoenzyme | Active apoenzyme + cofactor complex |
| Substrate | The molecule the enzyme acts on |
| Active site | Small pocket whose shape fits the substrate |

### 8.2 Properties of enzymes (exam favourite — "any four")

1. **Proteinaceous** (except ribozymes); denatured by heat and extreme pH.
2. **Catalytic** — huge turnover numbers; not consumed; needed in tiny amounts.
3. **Specific** — usually one enzyme for one substrate or one reaction type.
4. **Work in mild conditions** — aqueous, near-neutral pH, moderate temperature.
5. **Reversible** — the same enzyme catalyses forward and reverse reactions.
6. **pH- and temperature-sensitive** — each enzyme has an optimum (human enzymes ≈ 37 °C; pepsin ≈ pH 2, trypsin ≈ pH 8).
7. **Can be inhibited** — by competitive and non-competitive inhibitors.
8. **Often require cofactors.**

### 8.3 How enzymes work — lowering the activation energy

Every reaction needs an energy barrier to be crossed — the **activation energy**. Enzymes provide an alternative reaction path with a **much lower activation energy**: substrate binds in the active site → strained **enzyme–substrate (ES) complex** forms → product is released and the enzyme is free again. **Enzymes never change the equilibrium or the energy released — they only change the speed.**

| Basis | Lock-and-key model (Fischer, 1894) | Induced-fit model (Koshland, 1959) |
|---|---|---|
| Active site shape | Rigid, pre-formed, exactly matches substrate | Flexible; changes shape on substrate binding |
| Binding | Perfect rigid fit | Substrate "induces" the fit |
| Modern validity | Explains high specificity only | Accepted model — explains specificity + catalytic strain |

### 8.4 Factors affecting enzyme activity

| Factor | Effect | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| Temperature | Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum (~37 °C in humans), then falls sharply | Heat denatures the protein beyond the optimum |
| pH | Each enzyme has a narrow optimum pH | Charged groups of active site change state at extreme pH |
| Substrate concentration | Rate rises until saturation, then plateaus | All active sites become occupied |
| Enzyme concentration | Rate rises proportionally (substrate in excess) | More active sites available |
| Products / inhibitors | Slow or stop the reaction | See below |

**Inhibition:**

| Basis | Competitive inhibition | Non-competitive inhibition |
|---|---|---|
| Inhibitor shape | Resembles the substrate | Structurally unrelated |
| Binding site | Active site (competes with substrate) | Allosteric site (elsewhere) |
| Effect of more substrate | Overcomes inhibition | No effect |
| Example | Malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase | Cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase's metal centre |

### 8.5 Classification (IUB — six major classes)

| Class | Reaction catalysed | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Oxidoreductases | Oxidation–reduction (electron transfer) | Dehydrogenases, oxidases |
| 2. Transferases | Transfer of a functional group | Transaminase, hexokinase |
| 3. Hydrolases | Hydrolysis | Amylase, lipase, pepsin |
| 4. Lyases | Remove/add groups without hydrolysis (form double bonds) | Decarboxylase, aldolase |
| 5. Isomerases | Rearrangement within a molecule | Triose phosphate isomerase |
| 6. Ligases | Join molecules using ATP energy | DNA ligase |

### 8.6 Enzymes vs inorganic catalysts; enzymes vs hormones

| Basis | Enzyme | Inorganic catalyst | Hormone |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nature | Protein (usually) | Usually metal or small inorganic molecule | Protein, steroid or amine |
| Origin | Made only by living cells | Man-made or mineral | Made by endocrine glands |
| Specificity | Very high | Low | Acts on target organs/cells |
| Works at | Mild temperature and pH | Often high temperature/pressure | Not a catalyst at all — it is a messenger |
| Consumption | Not consumed | Not consumed | Consumed/broken after action |

**Immobilised enzymes** are enzymes attached to an inert solid support — they can be reused, recovered easily and used continuously in industry (glucose isomerase for high-fructose syrup) — the NEB 2021 question asks their advantage.

## 9. Water — The Medium of Life

Water makes up **70–90% of most cells** (a jellyfish ~95%; a human ~65%). Life almost certainly evolved in water, and every biological reaction happens in it.

### 9.1 Why water is so special — the properties

| Property | Cause | Biological importance |
|---|---|---|
| Excellent solvent | Polarity — O is slightly negative, H slightly positive; H-bonds surround ions and polar molecules | Blood, cytoplasm and sap are aqueous solutions; transport of nutrients, gases, wastes |
| High specific heat | Much absorbed energy breaks H-bonds before temperature rises | Body temperature stays stable; aquatic habitats are thermally stable |
| High heat of vaporization | H-bonds must be broken to evaporate | Sweating and transpiration cool organisms |
| Cohesion and adhesion | H-bonding between water molecules and to walls | Capillary rise in xylem; water column does not break |
| Density anomaly (max at 4 °C) | Ice forms an open lattice and floats | Ice insulates ponds; aquatic life survives winter |
| High surface tension | Cohesion at the surface | Water striders walk on water; droplet formation |
| Transparency | — | Light penetrates water — photosynthesis underwater |
| Reactant | Participates in hydrolysis and photosynthesis | Digestion and photosynthesis literally consume water |

### 9.2 Forms and roles

- **Free water:** bulk water in vacuoles, blood, tissue fluid — solvent and transport medium.
- **Bound water:** water attached to proteins and other macromolecules — gives them their shape and protects seeds/spores during drying.
- Roles: **medium of reactions, reactant (hydrolysis, photosynthesis), transport, temperature buffer, lubricant (joints, saliva), support (turgor, amniotic fluid), and dispersal medium for gametes in many aquatic species.**

## 10. Master Comparison Tables

### 10.1 The four great macromolecules side by side

| Basis | Carbohydrates | Proteins | Lipids | Nucleic acids |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elements | C, H, O | C, H, O, N (+S) | C, H, O (P, N in phospholipids) | C, H, O, N, P |
| Monomer | Monosaccharide | Amino acid | Glycerol + fatty acids (not a true polymer) | Nucleotide |
| Bond | Glycosidic | Peptide | Ester | Phosphodiester |
| Energy yield | 4 kcal/g | 4 kcal/g | 9 kcal/g | — (information, not fuel) |
| Main function | Immediate energy + structure | Catalysis, structure, transport, defence | Stored energy, membranes, hormones | Heredity and its expression |
| Example | Glucose, starch, cellulose | Haemoglobin, insulin, collagen | Triglyceride, cholesterol | DNA, mRNA |

### 10.2 Qualitative tests — identify the biomolecule

| Test | Detects | Positive result |

## 11. Conceptual Relationships — How This Topic Connects to Everything Else

- **Carbohydrates ↔ photosynthesis and respiration:** glucose is made in photosynthesis and broken in respiration; the pentose sugar ribose reappears in RNA.
- **Proteins ↔ enzymes and genetics:** enzymes are proteins; proteins are made according to the code in nucleic acids — so DNA ultimately controls every biomolecule (the central dogma).
- **Lipids ↔ cell membrane:** the phospholipid bilayer is the structural theme of Topic 3 (eukaryotic cell structure); membranes only work because of amphipathic lipid behaviour.
- **Nucleic acids ↔ cell division:** chromosomes = DNA + histone proteins; mitosis and meiosis (Topic 4) distribute DNA.
- **Minerals and water ↔ every physiological process:** nerve impulses (Na⁺/K⁺), oxygen transport (Fe in haemoglobin), photosynthesis (Mg in chlorophyll), and the fact that all reactions need an aqueous medium.
- **Ecology connection:** the 4 and 9 kcal/g energy values are exactly why energy pyramids shrink so fast — energy is lost at every trophic level as heat.
- **Health connection:** balanced diet = correct proportions of all biomolecule classes; deficiencies (anaemia, goitre, kwashiorkor, rickets) are mineral/protein deficiencies.

### 12.2 Model answers (exam-style, marks-proportioned)

**Q1 (3m) — Main classes of biomolecules with one function each.**
Answer: Biomolecules are the organic and inorganic compounds that make up living cells. (i) **Carbohydrates** — main energy source and structural material (cellulose). (ii) **Proteins** — growth, repair, catalysis (enzymes) and defence (antibodies). (iii) **Lipids** — concentrated energy storage (9 kcal/g) and membrane structure. (iv) **Nucleic acids** — storage and transmission of hereditary information (DNA, RNA). (v) **Enzymes** — protein catalysts that speed up metabolism. (vi) **Minerals and water** — regulate osmotic balance, act as cofactors and provide the reaction medium. *(Write definition + 4–6 classes + one clear function each; ½–½ marks per class with function.)*

**Q2 (3m) — Structure of a nucleotide and its role in DNA.**
Answer: A nucleotide has three components: (1) a **pentose sugar** — deoxyribose in DNA; (2) a **nitrogenous base** — purine (adenine/guanine) or pyrimidine (cytosine/thymine); (3) a **phosphate group**. Sugar + base = nucleoside; adding phosphate makes a nucleotide. In DNA, nucleotides join by **phosphodiester bonds** into long polynucleotide chains; the sequence of bases stores genetic information, and complementary base pairing (A=T, G≡C) allows exact replication and transmission of heredity.

**Q3 (4m) — Salient features of the Watson–Crick model.**
Answer: (1) DNA consists of two polynucleotide chains wound into a right-handed **double helix**; (2) the chains run **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′); (3) sugar–phosphate backbones lie **outside**, bases **inside**; (4) bases pair specifically — **A with T (2 H-bonds), G with C (3 H-bonds)** — a purine with a pyrimidine; (5) the strands are **complementary**, permitting semiconservative replication; (6) one turn = 3.4 nm with 10 base pairs; helix diameter 2 nm. *(Keywords: double helix, antiparallel, complementary, hydrogen bonds, 3.4 nm.)*

**Q4 (3m) — Enzymes: chemical nature and biocatalysts.**
Answer: Enzymes are chemically **proteins** (globular proteins; a few are catalytic RNAs). They are called **biocatalysts** because they are produced by living cells and accelerate biochemical reactions enormously — without being consumed or permanently changed — by lowering the activation energy, under mild conditions of temperature and pH.

**Q5 (3m) — Temperature and pH effects + immobilised enzymes.**
Answer: **Temperature:** enzyme activity rises with temperature up to an optimum (~37 °C in humans) because molecules collide more often; above the optimum, heat denatures the protein's tertiary structure and activity collapses. **pH:** each enzyme has a narrow optimum (pepsin ~2, trypsin ~8); at extreme pH the ionic charges of the active site change, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is denatured. **Advantage of immobilised enzymes:** they are fixed to an inert support so they can be **reused many times**, recovered easily from products, and used continuously in industrial bioreactors — cheaper and cleaner.

**Q6 (2m) — Classify carbohydrates with one example each.**
Answer: (1) **Monosaccharides** — single sugar unit — glucose; (2) **Disaccharides** — two units — sucrose; (3) **Oligosaccharides** — 3–10 units — raffinose; (4) **Polysaccharides** — many units — starch/cellulose.

**Q7 (3m) — Saturated vs unsaturated fatty acids; why bilayers form.**
Answer: **Saturated** fatty acids have only C–C single bonds, carry maximum hydrogen, are straight, pack tightly and are solid at room temperature (ghee, palmitic acid). **Unsaturated** fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds, are bent (kinked), pack loosely and are liquid oils at room temperature (mustard oil, oleic acid). **Phospholipid bilayers:** phospholipids are **amphipathic** — hydrophilic phosphate heads and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails. In water the heads face outward toward water while the tails hide from it, so two layers arrange tail-to-tail, forming the stable bilayer that is the basis of all cell membranes.

**Q8 (2m) — DNA vs RNA.**
Answer: DNA has **deoxyribose**, is **double-stranded**, uses **thymine**, is very **stable**, and **stores heredity**; RNA has **ribose**, is usually **single-stranded**, uses **uracil**, is **less stable**, and helps in **protein synthesis** (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA).

### 12.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Calling lipids "true polymers" — they are not; fatty acids are not repeated monomers.
2. Writing "RNA has thymine" — RNA uses **uracil**.
3. Confusing **nucleoside** (sugar + base) with **nucleotide** (sugar + base + phosphate).
4. Saying enzymes "provide energy" — they only **lower activation energy**; they never supply energy or change equilibrium.
5. Forgetting that denaturation does **not** break peptide bonds.
6. Reversing A=T (2 bonds) and G≡C (3 bonds) hydrogen-bond counts.
7. Saying the camel's hump stores water — it stores **fat** (which yields metabolic water when oxidised).

**Denaturation vs digestion:** denaturation (heat, pH) destroys 3-D shape but leaves peptide bonds intact; hydrolysis (digestion) actually breaks peptide bonds into amino acids.

**Starch vs glycogen vs cellulose:** all are glucose polymers, but starch (plants, α-1,4/1,6), glycogen (animals, more highly branched), cellulose (β-1,4, indigestible). Same monomer, different bonds = different biology.
**Competitive vs non-competitive inhibition:** competitive inhibitors bind the active site and can be overcome by more substrate; non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site and cannot.
**Enzyme vs hormone:** enzymes are catalysts (not consumed, act locally on substrates); hormones are chemical messengers (consumed after action, transported by blood to distant targets).
**DNA "contains protein":** DNA is pure nucleic acid; chromosomes contain DNA + histone protein. DNA itself has no protein.
**Saturated fat vs cholesterol:** saturation describes fatty-acid bonds; cholesterol is a steroid (derived lipid), a separate thing — both raise heart-disease risk but are chemically different.

## 1. Topic Introduction — What Are Biomolecules and Why Do They Matter?

**Biomolecules** are the carbon-based chemical compounds that make up every living cell and carry out every process we call "life". A cell is not a bag of random chemicals — it is a highly organised factory built from a small, special set of molecules: **carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, minerals, enzymes and water**.

Why this topic is the foundation of all of Biology:

- **Structure:** every cell wall, membrane, cytoskeleton and chromosome is built from biomolecules.
- **Energy:** every beat of your heart, every nerve impulse and every cell division is powered by the chemical energy stored in carbohydrates and lipids.
- **Information:** nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) store and translate the hereditary instructions that make a mango tree a mango tree and you, you.
- **Regulation:** enzymes (proteins) control the speed of every chemical reaction; minerals and water create the environment in which those reactions can happen.
- **Connection to the syllabus:** this topic directly feeds into *cell structure* (membranes are phospholipids + proteins), *cell division* (chromosomes are DNA + proteins), *enzymes* (all of metabolism), and later units like *ecology* (energy flow is chemical energy flowing through biomolecules).

**Where biomolecules come from:** almost all biomolecules are ultimately built by **photosynthesis**, which converts CO₂ and H₂O into glucose. Animals cannot make all of their own biomolecules from scratch — they must eat plants or other animals. This is why biomolecules are also the chemical basis of **food chains**.

## 2. Fundamental Conceptual Understanding — The Chemical Basis of Life

### 2.1 The elements of life

Over 99% of living matter is made of just six elements: **C, H, O, N, P, S** (remember: **CHNOPS**), plus minerals in smaller amounts.

| Element | Role in biomolecules |
|---|---|
| Carbon (C) | Backbone of all organic molecules — forms 4 stable covalent bonds |
| Hydrogen (H) | Part of every organic molecule; electron carrier in respiration |
| Oxygen (O) | Oxidation, water, carbohydrates, energy release |
| Nitrogen (N) | Amino acids, proteins, nucleic acid bases |
| Phosphorus (P) | Nucleic acids, ATP, phospholipids, bone |
| Sulphur (S) | Some amino acids (cysteine, methionine), protein shape |

**Why carbon?** Carbon has exactly 4 valence electrons, so it can form four strong covalent bonds, bond to itself in chains and rings, and build enormous, stable yet versatile molecules. Silicon, the closest alternative, forms weaker bonds and cannot build the diversity of molecules life needs. This is the deepest reason life is carbon-based.

### 2.2 The monomer → polymer principle

Almost every large biomolecule (macromolecule) is a **polymer** — a chain of repeated small units called **monomers**, joined by a specific covalent bond.

| Biomolecule class | Monomer (building block) | Polymer / large form | Bond joining monomers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrates | Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose) | Disaccharides, polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) | Glycosidic bond |
| Proteins | Amino acids (20 standard types) | Polypeptides → proteins | Peptide bond (−CO−NH−) |
| Lipids | Glycerol + fatty acids | Triglycerides, phospholipids | Ester bond (−COO−) |
| Nucleic acids | Nucleotides | DNA, RNA | Phosphodiester bond |

**Key conceptual point:** lipids (triglycerides) are *often listed* with the macromolecules but are **not true polymers** — fatty acids are not repeated identical monomers joined head-to-tail the way glucose or amino acids are. This is a favourite NEB trick question.

### 2.3 How polymers are built and broken: condensation and hydrolysis

- **Condensation (dehydration synthesis):** two monomers are joined and one molecule of **water is removed**. Building reactions — e.g. glucose + glucose → maltose + H₂O.
- **Hydrolysis:** water is added to split the polymer back into monomers. Breaking reactions — digestion is entirely hydrolysis.

$$\text{monomer}_1\text{–OH} + \text{HO–monomer}_2 \;\xrightarrow{\text{condensation}}\; \text{monomer}_1\text{–monomer}_2 + H_2O$$

**Cause and effect:** condensation requires energy (anabolic, enzyme-driven), hydrolysis releases it (catabolic). A polypeptide of *n* amino acids contains **(n − 1)** peptide bonds and loses **(n − 1)** water molecules during synthesis — a standard numerical asked in NEB exams.

### 2.4 Organic vs inorganic compounds in the cell

| Basis | Organic compounds | Inorganic compounds |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Carbon-based compounds (except simple ones like CO₂, carbonates) associated with living systems | Compounds without carbon skeletons (water, minerals, salts, gases) |
| Examples | Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, enzymes, vitamins | Water, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Fe²⁺, PO₄³⁻, O₂, CO₂ |
| Size | Usually large, complex macromolecules | Usually small, simple molecules or ions |
| Burning / combustion | Burn to give CO₂ + H₂O + energy | Generally do not burn |
| Function in cell | Build structures, store information, catalyse reactions, store energy | Provide medium, pH balance, osmotic balance, cofactors |
| Percentage of cell | ~20–30% (dry weight mostly organic) | Water alone is 70–90% of a cell |

## 3. Carbohydrates — The Primary Energy and Structural Molecules

### 3.1 Definition and general formula

**Carbohydrates** are organic compounds of **C, H and O** in which hydrogen and oxygen occur in the same 2:1 ratio as in water. General formula: **Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ** — e.g. glucose C₆H₁₂O₆, sucrose C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. They are also called **saccharides** (Greek *sakcharon* = sugar). They are the **first products of photosynthesis** and the main immediate fuel of respiration.

### 3.2 Classification of carbohydrates

| Class | Number of sugar units | Solubility / taste | Examples | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monosaccharides | 1 (cannot be hydrolysed) | Soluble, sweet, crystalline | Glucose, fructose, galactose, ribose | Immediate energy currency; monomers of all carbohydrates |
| Disaccharides | 2 (one glycosidic bond) | Soluble, sweet, crystalline | Maltose (glc+glc), sucrose (glc+fru), lactose (glc+gal) | Transport sugars (sucrose in plants), milk sugar (lactose) |
| Oligosaccharides | 3–10 | Partially soluble | Raffinose, stachyose | Cell-recognition markers on membrane surfaces |
| Polysaccharides | >10 (hundreds–thousands) | Insoluble or colloidal, tasteless | Starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin, inulin | Energy storage and structural materials |

**Monosaccharides are further classified by carbon number:**

| Carbon number | Name | Example | Importance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | Triose | Glyceraldehyde | Intermediate of respiration (glycolysis) |
| 5 | Pentose | Ribose, deoxyribose | Sugars of RNA and DNA |
| 6 | Hexose | Glucose, fructose, galactose | Main metabolic fuel |
| 7 | Heptose | Sedoheptulose | Photosynthesis (Calvin cycle) intermediate |

### 3.3 The glycosidic bond and how disaccharides form

A **glycosidic bond** is the C–O–C covalent link formed between two monosaccharides by **condensation**, catalysed by enzymes. Glucose + glucose → maltose + H₂O; glucose + fructose → sucrose; glucose + galactose → lactose.

### 3.4 Reducing vs non-reducing sugars — a guaranteed exam comparison

| Basis | Reducing sugars | Non-reducing sugars |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Have a free (or potentially free) aldehyde or ketone group that can reduce Cu²⁺ | No free aldehyde/ketone group; the anomeric carbons are locked in the glycosidic bond |
| Examples | All monosaccharides (glucose, fructose), maltose, lactose | Sucrose, all polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) |
| Benedict's / Fehling's test | Positive — brick-red Cu₂O precipitate | Negative (sucrose must first be hydrolysed, then it turns positive) |
| Biological role | Readily oxidised in respiration | Storage or transport forms (sucrose is non-reducing so it does not react while being transported in phloem) |

### 3.5 Storage vs structural polysaccharides

| Basis | Storage polysaccharides | Structural polysaccharides |
|---|---|---|
| Function | Energy reserve, broken down when glucose is needed | Mechanical support and protection |
| Examples | Starch (plants), glycogen (animals, liver + muscle), inulin (dahlia tubers) | Cellulose (plant cell wall), chitin (fungal wall, arthropod exoskeleton), peptidoglycan (bacterial wall) |
| Glucose linkage | α-1,4 and α-1,6 glycosidic bonds (α configuration) | β-1,4 glycosidic bonds (β configuration) |
| Digestibility | Human-digestible (we have α-amylase) | Not digestible by humans (we lack cellulase) — cellulose is "roughage/fibre" |
| Iodine test | Starch: blue-black; glycogen: reddish-brown | No colour with iodine |

**Conceptual insight:** the *only* chemical difference between digestible starch and indigestible cellulose is the **α vs β configuration** of the glycosidic bond — a beautiful example of how molecular geometry controls biology.

### 3.6 Functions of carbohydrates

1. **Energy source:** 4 kcal/g; glucose is the universal fuel of respiration.
2. **Energy storage:** starch (plants), glycogen (animals).
3. **Structural material:** cellulose in cell walls, chitin in fungi and arthropods.
4. **Precursors:** carbon skeletons for amino acids, fatty acids, nucleotides.
5. **Transport:** sucrose moves food through phloem.
6. **Cell recognition:** oligosaccharides on cell surfaces (blood groups, immunity).
7. **Component of nucleic acids:** ribose and deoxyribose.

## 4. Proteins — The Working Molecules of the Cell

### 4.1 Definition and building blocks

**Proteins** are large polymers of **amino acids** joined by **peptide bonds**. The word comes from Greek *proteios* = "of first importance" (coined by Berzelius). Proteins make up ~50% of a cell's dry weight and perform more different jobs than any other biomolecule class.

**Amino acid structure:** every standard amino acid has a central (α-) carbon bonded to four groups:

1. An **amino group** (−NH₂) — basic
2. A **carboxyl group** (−COOH) — acidic
3. A **hydrogen atom**
4. A variable **R-group (side chain)** — this alone defines which amino acid it is

Because of the amino and carboxyl groups, amino acids are **amphoteric** — they act as both acid and base, existing as **zwitterions** in solution. There are **20 standard amino acids**; humans cannot synthesise about 9–10 of them (**essential amino acids** — must come from diet, e.g. lysine, tryptophan, methionine).

### 4.2 The peptide bond — how proteins form

The −COOH of one amino acid condenses with the −NH₂ of the next, releasing water and forming the **peptide bond (−CO−NH−)**:

$$H_2N\text{–}CH(R)\text{–}COOH + H_2N\text{–}CH(R')\text{–}COOH \rightarrow H_2N\text{–}CH(R)\text{–}CO\text{–}NH\text{–}CH(R')\text{–}COOH + H_2O$$

Two amino acids → **dipeptide**; many → **polypeptide**; one or more folded polypeptides → **protein**. A chain of *n* amino acids has **(n − 1)** peptide bonds.

### 4.3 The four levels of protein structure

| Level | What it is | Bonds involved | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | The linear sequence of amino acids (covalent chain) | Peptide bonds | Insulin's 51-amino-acid sequence |
| Secondary | Local coiling/folding of the chain | Hydrogen bonds | α-helix (keratin), β-pleated sheet (silk fibroin) |
| Tertiary | Overall 3-D shape of one whole polypeptide | H-bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide (S–S) bridges, hydrophobic interactions | Myoglobin, enzymes |
| Quaternary | Assembly of 2 or more polypeptide subunits | Same non-covalent forces between subunits | Haemoglobin (4 subunits), insulin (2 chains) |

**Key concept:** **structure determines function.** Change the sequence (primary structure) — as in sickle-cell anaemia, where one wrong amino acid in haemoglobin's β-chain changes the whole shape — and the protein's function collapses.

### 4.4 Classification of proteins

| Main category | Subcategory | Characteristics | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simple proteins | Albumins, globulins, histones, glutelins | Only amino acids on hydrolysis | Egg albumin, serum globulin, histones of chromosomes |
| Conjugated proteins | Glycoproteins, lipoproteins, phosphoproteins, chromoproteins, metalloproteins, nucleoproteins | Protein + a non-protein **prosthetic group** | Mucin (glyco-), lipoproteins of membranes, casein (phospho-), haemoglobin (chromo-: haem + globin), nucleoproteins of chromosomes |
| Derived proteins | Proteoses, peptones, peptides | Partial breakdown products of proteins | Peptones formed during digestion |

### 4.5 Functions of proteins (with examples — learn the pairing)

| Function | Explanation | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Enzymatic (catalytic) | Speed up every metabolic reaction | Amylase, pepsin, DNA polymerase |
| Transport | Carry molecules in blood/membranes | Haemoglobin (O₂), membrane carriers |
| Structural | Build body and cell frameworks | Collagen, keratin, elastin |
| Contractile | Movement, muscle contraction | Actin, myosin |
| Hormonal | Chemical messengers | Insulin, growth hormone |
| Defensive | Immunity | Antibodies (immunoglobulins) |
| Storage | Nutrient reservoirs | Ovalbumin (egg), zein (maize) |
| Toxic / protective | Defence molecules | Snake venom, ricin |
| Buffering | Resist pH change in blood | Plasma proteins, haemoglobin |

### 4.6 Denaturation

**Denaturation** is the loss of a protein's natural 3-D structure (secondary → quaternary) by heat, pH extremes, or chemicals — **peptide bonds are NOT broken**, so the primary sequence survives, but the protein loses its biological activity (boiled egg; curdled milk). Renaturation is possible in some proteins if the denaturing agent is removed.

**Tests:** Biuret test (violet colour — peptide bonds), Xanthoproteic test (yellow with HNO₃ — aromatic amino acids), Million's test (for tyrosine).

## 5. Lipids — Concentrated Energy and Membrane Bricks

### 5.1 Definition

**Lipids** are a heterogeneous group of organic compounds that are **insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents** (ether, chloroform, benzene). They contain C, H, O — but with far less oxygen than carbohydrates, which is why they yield **more than twice the energy (9 kcal/g vs 4 kcal/g)** on oxidation.

### 5.2 Classification of lipids

| Main category | What it is | Examples | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simple lipids | Esters of fatty acids with alcohols | Fats (glycerol + fatty acids = triglycerides), waxes (fatty acid + long-chain alcohol, e.g. beeswax, cuticle wax) | Energy storage; waterproofing |
| Compound (conjugated) lipids | Lipid + non-lipid group | Phospholipids (phosphate + nitrogen base), glycolipids (carbohydrate), lipoproteins (protein) | Membrane structure; blood lipid transport |
| Derived lipids | Products of hydrolysis of simple/compound lipids | Fatty acids, glycerol, steroids (cholesterol, oestrogen, testosterone), terpenes (vitamin A, K, carotenoids) | Hormones, vitamins, membranes |

### 5.3 Fatty acids — saturated vs unsaturated (guaranteed exam table)

| Basis | Saturated fatty acids | Unsaturated fatty acids |
|---|---|---|
| Carbon–carbon bonds | Only single bonds (C–C) | One or more double bonds (C=C) |
| Hydrogen atoms | Maximum possible ("saturated" with H) | Fewer H atoms |
| Physical state at room temp | Solid fats (straight chains pack tightly) | Liquid oils (kinks prevent tight packing) |
| Source | Animal fats — ghee, butter, lard | Plant oils — mustard, sunflower, fish oil |
| Health effect | Raise blood cholesterol, linked to heart disease | Considered healthier; essential fatty acids (linoleic, linolenic) cannot be synthesised by humans |
| Example | Palmitic acid (C₁₆), stearic acid (C₁₈) | Oleic acid (C₁₈, one double bond), linoleic acid (two double bonds) |

### 5.4 Triglycerides — the storage fat

One **glycerol** (a 3-carbon alcohol with 3 −OH groups) + **3 fatty acids** → **triglyceride** + 3 H₂O, via three **ester bonds (−COO−)**. Stored in adipose tissue; the body's most concentrated energy reserve.

### 5.5 Phospholipids — why membranes form (conceptual core)

A phospholipid = glycerol + 2 fatty acids + **phosphate group + nitrogen base**. It is **amphipathic**: a **hydrophilic (water-loving) phosphate head** and **two hydrophobic (water-fearing) fatty-acid tails**. In water, heads face the water and tails hide from it — so phospholipids spontaneously form a **bilayer**, the universal framework of every biological membrane. This directly explains why the fluid-mosaic membrane exists (connect to Topic 3).

### 5.6 Functions of lipids

1. **Concentrated energy storage** — 9 kcal/g; 1 g fat ≈ energy of ~2.25 g carbohydrate.
2. **Membrane structure** — phospholipid bilayer.
3. **Insulation and padding** — subcutaneous fat conserves heat and cushions organs.
4. **Hormones and vitamins** — steroid hormones (oestrogen, testosterone, cortisol); fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K.
5. **Waterproofing** — waxes on leaf cuticles, skin oils.
6. **Electrical insulation** — myelin sheath (lipid) around neurons.
7. **Metabolic water** — oxidised fat yields metabolic water (desert animals, camel hump — the hump stores fat, not water).

**Tests:** Sudan III / IV stain (red), translucent-spot test on paper, saponification (soap formation with NaOH).

## 6. Nucleic Acids — The Information Molecules

### 6.1 Definition and the nucleotide

**Nucleic acids** (DNA and RNA) are polymers of **nucleotides** — the molecules that store, transmit and express hereditary information. First isolated by **Friedrich Miescher (1868–69)** from pus cells as "nuclein".

Every nucleotide has **three parts**:

1. A **pentose sugar** — ribose (RNA) or deoxyribose (DNA, missing one O on C-2′)
2. A **nitrogenous base** — purines (**Adenine, Guanine** — double ring) or pyrimidines (**Cytosine, Thymine, Uracil** — single ring)
3. A **phosphate group** — gives the molecule its acidic character

**Nucleoside = sugar + base. Nucleotide = sugar + base + phosphate.** Nucleotides join by **phosphodiester bonds** between the sugar of one and the phosphate of the next, forming a sugar–phosphate backbone with bases sticking inward.

**ATP (adenosine triphosphate)** is itself a nucleotide — proof that nucleotides are also the energy currency of the cell, not just genetic material.

### 6.2 DNA vs RNA — the master comparison (asked almost every year)

| Basis | DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) | RNA (ribonucleic acid) |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | Deoxyribose | Ribose |
| Strands | Double-stranded (double helix) | Usually single-stranded |
| Bases | A, G, C, **T** (thymine) | A, G, C, **U** (uracil replaces thymine) |
| Location | Mainly nucleus (also mitochondria, chloroplasts) | Nucleus and cytoplasm (ribosomes) |
| Function | Stores hereditary information; self-replicating | Transfers information from DNA to ribosomes; helps protein synthesis |
| Stability | Very stable (deoxyribose + thymine resist damage) | Less stable, short-lived |
| Types | One basic type (but different helix forms) | mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snRNA |
| Length | Very long (millions of nucleotides) | Much shorter |
| Base pairing | A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds) | A=U, G≡C |

### 6.3 Watson–Crick double-helix model (1953) — salient features

1. DNA is a **double helix** of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands (one 5′→3′, the other 3′→5′).
2. The **sugar–phosphate backbones face outside**; the bases pair **inside** the helix.
3. **Complementary base pairing:** A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds), G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds) — a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, keeping the helix a uniform 2 nm wide.
4. The two strands are **complementary** — knowing one sequence fixes the other; this is the physical basis of accurate replication.
5. One complete turn occurs every **3.4 nm** with **10 base pairs per turn**.
6. **Chargaff's rule:** in any DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C (follows directly from pairing).

### 6.4 Types and roles of RNA

| RNA type | Full form | Role |
|---|---|---|
| mRNA | Messenger RNA | Carries the genetic code from DNA to the ribosome |
| tRNA | Transfer RNA | Brings specific amino acids to the ribosome; reads the code |
| rRNA | Ribosomal RNA | Structural + catalytic core of ribosomes |
| snRNA | Small nuclear RNA | RNA splicing in eukaryotes |

### 6.5 Functions of nucleic acids

1. **Storage of genetic information** (DNA).
2. **Transmission of heredity** from parents to offspring and cell to daughter cell.
3. **Expression of information** — DNA → RNA → protein (the central dogma).
4. **Mutation and evolution** — changes in DNA sequence create variation.
5. **Energy transfer** — ATP, NAD, FAD are nucleotide derivatives.

**Test:** diphenylamine reagent turns blue with DNA (Dische test).

## 7. Minerals — The Inorganic Regulators

Minerals are inorganic elements needed in small amounts. They come from food and soil (plants absorb them as ions) and act as **structural materials, cofactors, and osmotic/electrolyte regulators**.

| Mineral (ion) | Category | Key functions | Deficiency effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calcium (Ca²⁺) | Macro | Bones, teeth, muscle contraction, blood clotting, cell-wall middle lamellum | Rickets, poor bones, poor clotting |
| Phosphorus (P) | Macro | ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids, bones | Weak bones, low energy metabolism |
| Iron (Fe²⁺) | Micro | Haemoglobin, cytochromes, chlorophyll synthesis (activator) | Anaemia |
| Iodine (I) | Micro | Thyroxine synthesis | Goitre |
| Sodium (Na⁺) / Potassium (K⁺) | Macro | Nerve impulse, osmotic balance, stomatal movement (K⁺) | Muscle cramps, poor nerve conduction |
| Magnesium (Mg²⁺) | Macro | Central atom of chlorophyll; enzyme activator | Chlorosis |
| Chlorine (Cl⁻) | Micro | Osmotic balance, HCl in gastric juice | Electrolyte imbalance |
| Zinc (Zn²⁺), Copper (Cu²⁺), Manganese (Mn) | Micro | Enzyme cofactors (e.g. Zn for carbonic anhydrase) | Poor growth, enzyme failure |

**Macro vs micro minerals:** macro minerals are needed in larger amounts (>100 mg/day, e.g. Ca, P, Na, K, Mg, Cl); micro (trace) elements are needed in traces but are still essential (Fe, I, Zn, Cu, Mn, Co, Se).

## 8. Enzymes — Biological Catalysts

### 8.1 Definition and nature

**Enzymes** are biological catalysts — almost always **globular proteins** (a few RNAs, "ribozymes", also catalyse) — that **accelerate biochemical reactions thousands to millions of times** without being consumed themselves. The term was coined by **Kühne (1878)**; **Sumner (1926)** crystallised the first enzyme, urease, and proved enzymes are protein.

**Terminology chain:** some enzymes need a non-protein helper to work:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Apoenzyme | The inactive protein part alone |
| Cofactor | Non-protein helper: metal ion (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺) |
| Coenzyme | Organic cofactor, often a vitamin derivative (NAD, FAD, coenzyme A) |
| Prosthetic group | Cofactor tightly/covalently bound to the apoenzyme |
| Holoenzyme | Active apoenzyme + cofactor complex |
| Substrate | The molecule the enzyme acts on |
| Active site | Small pocket whose shape fits the substrate |

### 8.2 Properties of enzymes (exam favourite — "any four")

1. **Proteinaceous** (except ribozymes); denatured by heat and extreme pH.
2. **Catalytic** — huge turnover numbers; not consumed; needed in tiny amounts.
3. **Specific** — usually one enzyme for one substrate or one reaction type.
4. **Work in mild conditions** — aqueous, near-neutral pH, moderate temperature.
5. **Reversible** — the same enzyme catalyses forward and reverse reactions.
6. **pH- and temperature-sensitive** — each enzyme has an optimum (human enzymes ≈ 37 °C; pepsin ≈ pH 2, trypsin ≈ pH 8).
7. **Can be inhibited** — by competitive and non-competitive inhibitors.
8. **Often require cofactors.**

### 8.3 How enzymes work — lowering the activation energy

Every reaction needs an energy barrier to be crossed — the **activation energy**. Enzymes provide an alternative reaction path with a **much lower activation energy**: substrate binds in the active site → strained **enzyme–substrate (ES) complex** forms → product is released and the enzyme is free again. **Enzymes never change the equilibrium or the energy released — they only change the speed.**

| Basis | Lock-and-key model (Fischer, 1894) | Induced-fit model (Koshland, 1959) |
|---|---|---|
| Active site shape | Rigid, pre-formed, exactly matches substrate | Flexible; changes shape on substrate binding |
| Binding | Perfect rigid fit | Substrate "induces" the fit |
| Modern validity | Explains high specificity only | Accepted model — explains specificity + catalytic strain |

### 8.4 Factors affecting enzyme activity

| Factor | Effect | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| Temperature | Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum (~37 °C in humans), then falls sharply | Heat denatures the protein beyond the optimum |
| pH | Each enzyme has a narrow optimum pH | Charged groups of active site change state at extreme pH |
| Substrate concentration | Rate rises until saturation, then plateaus | All active sites become occupied |
| Enzyme concentration | Rate rises proportionally (substrate in excess) | More active sites available |
| Products / inhibitors | Slow or stop the reaction | See below |

**Inhibition:**

| Basis | Competitive inhibition | Non-competitive inhibition |
|---|---|---|
| Inhibitor shape | Resembles the substrate | Structurally unrelated |
| Binding site | Active site (competes with substrate) | Allosteric site (elsewhere) |
| Effect of more substrate | Overcomes inhibition | No effect |
| Example | Malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase | Cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase's metal centre |

### 8.5 Classification (IUB — six major classes)

| Class | Reaction catalysed | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Oxidoreductases | Oxidation–reduction (electron transfer) | Dehydrogenases, oxidases |
| 2. Transferases | Transfer of a functional group | Transaminase, hexokinase |
| 3. Hydrolases | Hydrolysis | Amylase, lipase, pepsin |
| 4. Lyases | Remove/add groups without hydrolysis (form double bonds) | Decarboxylase, aldolase |
| 5. Isomerases | Rearrangement within a molecule | Triose phosphate isomerase |
| 6. Ligases | Join molecules using ATP energy | DNA ligase |

### 8.6 Enzymes vs inorganic catalysts; enzymes vs hormones

| Basis | Enzyme | Inorganic catalyst | Hormone |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nature | Protein (usually) | Usually metal or small inorganic molecule | Protein, steroid or amine |
| Origin | Made only by living cells | Man-made or mineral | Made by endocrine glands |
| Specificity | Very high | Low | Acts on target organs/cells |
| Works at | Mild temperature and pH | Often high temperature/pressure | Not a catalyst at all — it is a messenger |
| Consumption | Not consumed | Not consumed | Consumed/broken after action |

**Immobilised enzymes** are enzymes attached to an inert solid support — they can be reused, recovered easily and used continuously in industry (glucose isomerase for high-fructose syrup) — the NEB 2021 question asks their advantage.

## 9. Water — The Medium of Life

Water makes up **70–90% of most cells** (a jellyfish ~95%; a human ~65%). Life almost certainly evolved in water, and every biological reaction happens in it.

### 9.1 Why water is so special — the properties

| Property | Cause | Biological importance |
|---|---|---|
| Excellent solvent | Polarity — O is slightly negative, H slightly positive; H-bonds surround ions and polar molecules | Blood, cytoplasm and sap are aqueous solutions; transport of nutrients, gases, wastes |
| High specific heat | Much absorbed energy breaks H-bonds before temperature rises | Body temperature stays stable; aquatic habitats are thermally stable |
| High heat of vaporization | H-bonds must be broken to evaporate | Sweating and transpiration cool organisms |
| Cohesion and adhesion | H-bonding between water molecules and to walls | Capillary rise in xylem; water column does not break |
| Density anomaly (max at 4 °C) | Ice forms an open lattice and floats | Ice insulates ponds; aquatic life survives winter |
| High surface tension | Cohesion at the surface | Water striders walk on water; droplet formation |
| Transparency | — | Light penetrates water — photosynthesis underwater |
| Reactant | Participates in hydrolysis and photosynthesis | Digestion and photosynthesis literally consume water |

### 9.2 Forms and roles

- **Free water:** bulk water in vacuoles, blood, tissue fluid — solvent and transport medium.
- **Bound water:** water attached to proteins and other macromolecules — gives them their shape and protects seeds/spores during drying.
- Roles: **medium of reactions, reactant (hydrolysis, photosynthesis), transport, temperature buffer, lubricant (joints, saliva), support (turgor, amniotic fluid), and dispersal medium for gametes in many aquatic species.**

## 11. Conceptual Relationships — How This Topic Connects to Everything Else

- **Carbohydrates ↔ photosynthesis and respiration:** glucose is made in photosynthesis and broken in respiration; the pentose sugar ribose reappears in RNA.
- **Proteins ↔ enzymes and genetics:** enzymes are proteins; proteins are made according to the code in nucleic acids — so DNA ultimately controls every biomolecule (the central dogma).
- **Lipids ↔ cell membrane:** the phospholipid bilayer is the structural theme of Topic 3 (eukaryotic cell structure); membranes only work because of amphipathic lipid behaviour.
- **Nucleic acids ↔ cell division:** chromosomes = DNA + histone proteins; mitosis and meiosis (Topic 4) distribute DNA.
- **Minerals and water ↔ every physiological process:** nerve impulses (Na⁺/K⁺), oxygen transport (Fe in haemoglobin), photosynthesis (Mg in chlorophyll), and the fact that all reactions need an aqueous medium.
- **Ecology connection:** the 4 and 9 kcal/g energy values are exactly why energy pyramids shrink so fast — energy is lost at every trophic level as heat.
- **Health connection:** balanced diet = correct proportions of all biomolecule classes; deficiencies (anaemia, goitre, kwashiorkor, rickets) are mineral/protein deficiencies.

### 12.2 Model answers (exam-style, marks-proportioned)

**Q1 (3m) — Main classes of biomolecules with one function each.**
Answer: Biomolecules are the organic and inorganic compounds that make up living cells. (i) **Carbohydrates** — main energy source and structural material (cellulose). (ii) **Proteins** — growth, repair, catalysis (enzymes) and defence (antibodies). (iii) **Lipids** — concentrated energy storage (9 kcal/g) and membrane structure. (iv) **Nucleic acids** — storage and transmission of hereditary information (DNA, RNA). (v) **Enzymes** — protein catalysts that speed up metabolism. (vi) **Minerals and water** — regulate osmotic balance, act as cofactors and provide the reaction medium. *(Write definition + 4–6 classes + one clear function each; ½–½ marks per class with function.)*

**Q2 (3m) — Structure of a nucleotide and its role in DNA.**
Answer: A nucleotide has three components: (1) a **pentose sugar** — deoxyribose in DNA; (2) a **nitrogenous base** — purine (adenine/guanine) or pyrimidine (cytosine/thymine); (3) a **phosphate group**. Sugar + base = nucleoside; adding phosphate makes a nucleotide. In DNA, nucleotides join by **phosphodiester bonds** into long polynucleotide chains; the sequence of bases stores genetic information, and complementary base pairing (A=T, G≡C) allows exact replication and transmission of heredity.

**Q3 (4m) — Salient features of the Watson–Crick model.**
Answer: (1) DNA consists of two polynucleotide chains wound into a right-handed **double helix**; (2) the chains run **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′); (3) sugar–phosphate backbones lie **outside**, bases **inside**; (4) bases pair specifically — **A with T (2 H-bonds), G with C (3 H-bonds)** — a purine with a pyrimidine; (5) the strands are **complementary**, permitting semiconservative replication; (6) one turn = 3.4 nm with 10 base pairs; helix diameter 2 nm. *(Keywords: double helix, antiparallel, complementary, hydrogen bonds, 3.4 nm.)*

**Q4 (3m) — Enzymes: chemical nature and biocatalysts.**
Answer: Enzymes are chemically **proteins** (globular proteins; a few are catalytic RNAs). They are called **biocatalysts** because they are produced by living cells and accelerate biochemical reactions enormously — without being consumed or permanently changed — by lowering the activation energy, under mild conditions of temperature and pH.

**Q5 (3m) — Temperature and pH effects + immobilised enzymes.**
Answer: **Temperature:** enzyme activity rises with temperature up to an optimum (~37 °C in humans) because molecules collide more often; above the optimum, heat denatures the protein's tertiary structure and activity collapses. **pH:** each enzyme has a narrow optimum (pepsin ~2, trypsin ~8); at extreme pH the ionic charges of the active site change, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is denatured. **Advantage of immobilised enzymes:** they are fixed to an inert support so they can be **reused many times**, recovered easily from products, and used continuously in industrial bioreactors — cheaper and cleaner.

**Q6 (2m) — Classify carbohydrates with one example each.**
Answer: (1) **Monosaccharides** — single sugar unit — glucose; (2) **Disaccharides** — two units — sucrose; (3) **Oligosaccharides** — 3–10 units — raffinose; (4) **Polysaccharides** — many units — starch/cellulose.

**Q7 (3m) — Saturated vs unsaturated fatty acids; why bilayers form.**
Answer: **Saturated** fatty acids have only C–C single bonds, carry maximum hydrogen, are straight, pack tightly and are solid at room temperature (ghee, palmitic acid). **Unsaturated** fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds, are bent (kinked), pack loosely and are liquid oils at room temperature (mustard oil, oleic acid). **Phospholipid bilayers:** phospholipids are **amphipathic** — hydrophilic phosphate heads and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails. In water the heads face outward toward water while the tails hide from it, so two layers arrange tail-to-tail, forming the stable bilayer that is the basis of all cell membranes.

**Q8 (2m) — DNA vs RNA.**
Answer: DNA has **deoxyribose**, is **double-stranded**, uses **thymine**, is very **stable**, and **stores heredity**; RNA has **ribose**, is usually **single-stranded**, uses **uracil**, is **less stable**, and helps in **protein synthesis** (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA).

### 12.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Calling lipids "true polymers" — they are not; fatty acids are not repeated monomers.
2. Writing "RNA has thymine" — RNA uses **uracil**.
3. Confusing **nucleoside** (sugar + base) with **nucleotide** (sugar + base + phosphate).
4. Saying enzymes "provide energy" — they only **lower activation energy**; they never supply energy or change equilibrium.
5. Forgetting that denaturation does **not** break peptide bonds.
6. Reversing A=T (2 bonds) and G≡C (3 bonds) hydrogen-bond counts.
7. Saying the camel's hump stores water — it stores **fat** (which yields metabolic water when oxidised).

### Extra depth — why these four classes matter together
The four classes interlock: nucleic acids (DNA) store the recipe, proteins (enzymes) execute it, carbohydrates supply the instant fuel the enzymes burn, and lipids warehouse the long-term reserve. A deficiency in any one breaks the chain — no vitamin-derived cofactor (minerals) means an enzyme cannot bind its substrate; no membrane lipids means the cell has no compartment to keep reactions ordered.
Water deserves special mention: it is the medium in which all four dissolve, react and transport — 70–90% of a cell's mass. Minerals (Na, K, Ca, Fe, Mg) are needed in milligrams yet without them haemoglobin, chlorophyll, nerve impulses and bone simply do not exist.

### Extra depth — tests that identify each class
Carbohydrates: Benedict's test (reducing sugars give brick-red Cu₂O on heating), iodine test (starch → blue-black). Proteins: Biuret test (violet with dilute CuSO₄ + NaOH), Xanthoproteic (yellow with conc. HNO₃). Lipids: Sudan III stains red; the translucent-spot test on paper. Nucleic acids: diphenylamine (DNA → blue), orcinol (RNA → green). These colour tests are standard 2–3 mark NEB questions — memorise reagent and colour together.
confusion: **Lipid vs carbohydrate as "polymer":** carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids are true polymers of repeated monomers; triglycerides are NOT — glycerol and fatty acids are different molecules, not repeated units. NEB loves this trap.
**Nucleoside vs nucleotide:** nucleoside = sugar + base only; nucleotide = sugar + base + phosphate. Only the nucleotide is the true monomer of nucleic acids.
**Denaturation vs digestion:** denaturation (heat, pH) destroys 3-D shape but leaves peptide bonds intact; hydrolysis (digestion) actually breaks peptide bonds into amino acids.

**Starch vs glycogen vs cellulose:** all are glucose polymers, but starch (plants, α-1,4/1,6), glycogen (animals, more highly branched), cellulose (β-1,4, indigestible). Same monomer, different bonds = different biology.
**Competitive vs non-competitive inhibition:** competitive inhibitors bind the active site and can be overcome by more substrate; non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site and cannot.
**Enzyme vs hormone:** enzymes are catalysts (not consumed, act locally on substrates); hormones are chemical messengers (consumed after action, transported by blood to distant targets).
**DNA "contains protein":** DNA is pure nucleic acid; chromosomes contain DNA + histone protein. DNA itself has no protein.
**Saturated fat vs cholesterol:** saturation describes fatty-acid bonds; cholesterol is a steroid (derived lipid), a separate thing — both raise heart-disease risk but are chemically different.

practiceQuestions: **Short answer (2m): Define biomolecules. Give two examples.** — Biomolecules are the organic and inorganic compounds that constitute living cells and take part in all life processes. Examples: glucose (carbohydrate), haemoglobin (protein); also lipids, nucleic acids, water, minerals.

**Short answer (2m): What is a peptide bond?** — The covalent bond (−CO−NH−) formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next by condensation, releasing water; it links amino acids into polypeptides.

**Short answer (2m): Why is water called the universal solvent?** — Because its polar molecules form hydrogen bonds and hydration shells around ions and polar compounds, dissolving more substances than any other liquid; this makes blood, cytoplasm and sap possible.

**Short answer (2m): What are coenzymes? Give one example.** — Small organic, non-protein cofactors (often vitamin derivatives) required by some apoenzymes for activity. Example: NAD, FAD, coenzyme A.

**Long answer (5m): Describe the classification of carbohydrates with examples and state their functions.** — Full answer: definition + general formula; four classes (mono-, di-, oligo-, polysaccharides) each with definition, examples and significance; storage vs structural polysaccharides (starch/glycogen vs cellulose/chitin); functions — energy (4 kcal/g), storage, structure, transport (sucrose), cell recognition, nucleic-acid sugars. Structure the answer as: definition → classification table → functions list.

**Long answer (5m): Describe the structure of DNA according to the Watson–Crick model.** — Double helix of two antiparallel strands; sugar–phosphate backbone outside, bases inside; complementary pairing A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds); purine–pyrimidine pairing keeps 2 nm diameter; 10 bp/turn, 3.4 nm/turn; complementarity explains semiconservative replication and Chargaff's rule. Include a labelled diagram.

**Long answer (5m): What are enzymes? Explain the factors affecting enzyme activity.** — Definition + protein nature + active site + ES complex + activation-energy lowering. Factors: temperature (optimum then denaturation), pH (narrow optimum), substrate concentration (saturation plateau), enzyme concentration (proportional rise), inhibitors (competitive vs non-competitive). Draw rate-vs-temperature and rate-vs-pH curves.

**Conceptual (3m): "Structure determines function." Justify this statement with two biomolecule examples.** — (1) Starch vs cellulose: identical glucose monomers, but α vs β glycosidic bonds make one digestible and the other structural fibre. (2) Haemoglobin: one amino-acid substitution in the β-chain (sickle-cell anaemia) changes the quaternary shape and destroys O₂-carrying efficiency. In both cases the 3-D arrangement — not the composition alone — decides the biological role.

**Conceptual (3m): Why are enzymes called biocatalysts but not "sources of energy"?** — Enzymes only lower the activation energy so reactions reach equilibrium faster; they are not consumed and they supply no energy themselves — the energy comes from the substrate's chemical bonds. A catalyst changes rate, never the ΔG or the equilibrium position.

**Application (3m): A patient's blood test shows low haemoglobin and an enlarged thyroid. Which minerals are deficient, and why?** — Low haemoglobin → **iron** deficiency (Fe²⁺ is the central atom of haem, the O₂-binding prosthetic group of haemoglobin) → anaemia. Enlarged thyroid → **iodine** deficiency (iodine is required to synthesise thyroxine; without it TSH keeps stimulating the thyroid, causing goitre).

**Application (2m): Why is sucrose, not glucose, the sugar transported in plant phloem?** — Sucrose is non-reducing and chemically inert, so it neither reacts with, nor is consumed by, the cells it passes through during long-distance transport; glucose would be metabolised or react en route.
